learningObjective: Create route tables and your own routes (UDRs), attach them to subnets, and predict which route Azure picks.
engineer: Route table: a list of routes. Each route says: traffic to this address range, send it to this next hop. You attach the table to one or more subnets (same region and subscription). A subnet can have only one route table.

Next hop types: Virtual appliance, the IP of a firewall or NVA (for example Azure Firewall); Virtual network gateway, the VPN or ExpressRoute gateway; Virtual network, stay inside the VNet; Internet; None, which drops the traffic.
How Azure picks a route, rule 1: the longest (most specific) prefix wins. A /24 beats a /16, which beats 0.0.0.0/0.
How Azure picks a route, rule 2: if prefixes are the same length, your own routes (UDRs) win, then BGP routes, then Azure's system routes.
NVAs must forward: turn on IP forwarding on the NVA's network card in Azure, and turn on forwarding inside its OS. Otherwise it drops traffic meant for other addresses.
Propagate gateway routes: turn this off on a route table to stop routes learned from on-premises (BGP) reaching the subnet. For example, to force all traffic through the firewall.
Service tags as destinations: a route's address can be a service tag, for example Storage.

example.title: Sending all internet traffic through Azure Firewall
body: Route table rt-spokes has one route: 0.0.0.0/0 → Virtual appliance 10.0.1.4 (Azure Firewall's private IP). It's attached to every spoke subnet. Now all internet traffic is checked and logged by the firewall before it leaves.

architectureDecisions: One exit to the internet: send 0.0.0.0/0 to Azure Firewall from every spoke.
Few route tables: share one table across similar subnets where you can.
Check after every change: look at Effective routes and run Next hop.

misconceptions.myth: Your own route (UDR) always beats a system route.
misconceptions.reality: No. Only when the prefixes are the same length. A longer prefix always wins first.

misconceptions.myth: Route tables are attached to network cards.

comparisons.difference: Also attached to subnets. Next hops are gateways, NAT, network interfaces (ENIs) or Transit Gateway.
Swaps routes with NVAs automatically using BGP, instead of you writing static routes.

troubleshooting.symptom: Traffic doesn't go through the firewall.
troubleshooting.cause: The route table isn't attached to the subnet, or a more specific system or BGP route wins.
troubleshooting.fix: Check Effective routes on the VM's network card (NIC).

troubleshooting.symptom: Traffic reaches the NVA but goes no further.
troubleshooting.cause: IP forwarding is off on the network card or inside the OS.

troubleshooting.symptom: Connections break because replies take a different path (asymmetric routing).
troubleshooting.cause: Return traffic skips the firewall, which tracks connections.
troubleshooting.fix: Add matching routes on the way back too.

configuration.permissions: Network Contributor on the resource group
